53: investigation.
54: It is worth mentioning that similar approach, taking advantage of tim e averaging, has
55: also been applied to the two-dimensional rotating inviscid Burgers eq uations in [1] and
56: [16] to show that fast rotation prevents the formation of a ﬁnite t ime singularity in the
57: two-dimensional Burgers system. We will use this warmup toy model, and in particular
58: the approach in [1], to ﬁx ideas and to illustrate in section 2 the averag ing mechanism,
59: which is instrumental in regularizing the solutions and in preventing th e formation of a
60: ﬁnite time singularity for the two-dimensional inviscid Burgers syste m.
61: Our approach consists of three steps. First, we rewrite the prob lem as a system of
62: ODE for time-dependent Fourier coeﬃcients. This is a standard app roach to the periodic
63: problem which is commonly used. Second, to make the eﬀects of time a veraging explicit
64: we single out oscillating factors and do several integration by parts , with respect to time,
65: to obtain several generations of equations for slowly varying coeﬃ cients. Resonances
66: reveal themselves as obstacles to the integrations by parts and p roduce resonant terms
67: in the equations, integrated terms become more and more regular. Higher generations of
68: equations allow solutions with less regularity. This algorithm is simple and straightforward,
69: it does not use ﬁne methods such as analytic reduction to linear form s and analysis of self
70: similar solutions or the construction of conserved or almost conser ved quantities. The third
71: step is analysis of the obtained equations. To show their regularity w e use straightforward
72: estimates of multilinear operators, energy estimates and the Cont raction principle. To use
73: the contraction principle in negative Sobolev spaces we use splitting t o high and low Fourier
74: modes and exploit averaging-induced squeezing of higher modes. In order to justify our
75: estimates we use a Galerkin approximations procedure. We try to us e methods which can
76: be easily adjusted to general multidimensional problems such as tho se mentioned above
77: in hydrodynamic problems. We do not use in our analysis the speciﬁc pr operties of the
78: KdV equation such as complete integrability or special conserved qu antities. Moreover,
79: one can expect that in order to obtain more delicate information one has to resort to the
80: use of higher generations of equations, i.e. more integrations by pa rt.
81: The paper is organized as follows. In section 3 we reformulate the Kd V equation in
82: terms of its Fourier components and introduce the notion of weak s olution; we also make
83: two types of formal transformations of the equation which will be u sed for proving the
84: relevant well-posedness results. In section 4 we use the Galerkin pr ocedure for proving the
85: global existence in the Sobolev spaces ˙H s for s >0. In section 5 we use the Contraction
86: Principle to show that the solutions established in section 4 are unique and Lipschitz
87: continuous, with respect to the initial data, in the Sobolev spaces ˙H s for s ≥ 1/2. A
88: more technical section 6 is devoted to proving similar results for s ∈ [0, 1/2], where the
89: case s = 0 is dealt with separately. Finally, for solutions with initial data in L2 we show
90: the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these solutions, with resp ect to the initial data,
91: as maps from ˙H s to ˙H s for all s ∈ (−1, 0].
92: There is a long history of the KdV equations in the periodical setting. We do not attempt
93: to give here a complete survey of this long history, but we are satisﬁ ed by mentioning,
94: below, some of the key landmark results. First Bourgain [6] proved local well-posedness in
95: L2. We observe that the result of Bourgain also implies global existence for the real valued
96: KdV in L2. Later the local well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s > −1/2, was
97: 
98: REGULARIZATION MECHANISM FOR THE PERIODIC KDV EQUATION 3
99: established for the real and complex valued KdV by Kenig, Ponce, an d Vega [14]. Later
100: global well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s> −1/2, was established for the real
101: valued KdV by Colliander, Keel, Staﬃlani, Takaoka and Tao [7]. Using th e fact that the
102: KdV equation is an integrable system, and by implementing the inverse method, Kappeler
103: and Topalov [15] proved global well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s> −1.
104: Even though the results presented in this contribution are weaker than the state-of-the-
105: art results mentioned above, our approach is substantially diﬀeren t and easy to master.
106: Speciﬁcally, and as we have stressed above, our approach is based on systematic applica-
107: tion of time averaging. It is worth mentioning that since we rewrite th e KdV equation
108: in diﬀerent forms, based on the diﬀerentiation by parts with respec t to the time variable,
109: there is superﬁcial similarity with the reduction to normal forms (cf . [19]). The diﬀerence
110: is that the consecutive forms of the KdV, which we derive, are base d not on the geometric
111: properties such as a reduction to a linear form or a reduction to inva riant tori, but ex-
112: clusively on time averaging properties. In order to stress the eﬀec ts, which are due solely
113: to the time averaging, we do not use energy conservation or modiﬁe d energy functionals
114: as in the I-method. We use only the L2 norm conservation to mimic the situation which
115: occurs in the three-dimensional Euler equations and other hydrod ynamical systems.
116: Moreover, we believe that the averaging approach presented her e can be pushed further
117: to achieve the best known results concerning the KdV equation. Fu rthermore, diﬀerent
118: nonlinear dispersive and wave equations, such as the m-KdV, the Kle in-Gordon equation
119: and water wave equations (see for example, [13], [19], [23]-[25], and re ferences therein),
120: can possibly be studied quite similarly, a subject of future research .

4: Communicated by Arieh Iserles
5: Abstract. This article is concerned with the construction and analysis of new time dis-
6: cretizations for the KdV equation on a torus for low-regularity solutions below H 1. New
7: harmonic analysis tools, including averaging approximations to the exponential phase func-
8: tions and trilinear estimates of the KdV operator, are established for the construction and
9: analysis of time discretizations with higher convergence orders under low-regularity condi-
10: tions. In addition, new perturbation techniques are introduced to establish stability estimates
11: of time discretizations under low-regularity conditions without using filters when the energy
12: techniques fail. The proposed method is proved to be convergent with order γ (up to a
13: logarithmic factor) in L2 under the regularity condition u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ) for γ ∈ (0, 1].
14: Keywords: KdV equation, rough data, low-regularity integrator, stability, error estimates

29: 1. Introduction
30: The Korteweg–De Vries (KdV) equation is a nonlinear dispersive partial differential equa-
31: tion that describes many physical phenomena, including shallow water waves, ion acoustic
32: 1
33: 
34: 2
35: waves in plasmas, acoustic waves on crystal lattices, and so on. The development of compu-
36: tational methods for the KdV equation has attracted much attention.
37: It is known that the KdV equation, either on a torus or on the whole space, is globally well-
38: posed in H s with s ≥ 0, i.e., there exists a unique solution in C([0, T]; H s) for any initial value
39: in H s; see [1,10,12,33]. However, classical time discretizations for the KdV equation, including
40: finite difference methods, splitting methods, discontinuous Galerkin methods, and classical
41: exponential integrators, generally require much higher regularity for the numerical solutions
42: to converge with certain orders, i.e., these methods typically require u ∈ C([0, T]; H 3) and
43: u ∈ C([0, T]; H 6) to have first- and second-order convergence in L2, respectively. The error
44: estimates under these regularity conditions (or stronger conditions) for the above-mentioned
45: classical time discretizations have been established, for example, in [7–9, 16, 17, 21, 25, 27, 32].
46: Such regularity conditions are not mere technical conditions required in the error analysis.
47: When the solution of the KdV equation does not have the required regularity, its numerical
48: approximations by the classical time discretizations generally have reduced order of conver-
49: gence.
50: In practice, the solutions of the KdV equation may be rough due to measurement or
51: randomness of the data [2, 5]. To address the numerical approximation to nonsmooth so-
52: lutions, some low-regularity exponential integrators based on resonance analysis were re-
53: cently developed to relax the regularity requirement in solving nonlinear dispersive equations.
54: Such low-regularity integrators based on resonance analysis were initially introduced by Hof-
55: manov´ a & Schratz [6] and Ostermann & Schratz [18, 20] for solving the KdV equation and
56: the nonlinear Schr¨ odinger (NLS) equation, respectively. In particular, for the KdV equa-
57: tion, the low-regularity integrator proposed in [6] can have first-order convergence in H 1 for
58: u ∈ C([0, T]; H 3). Wu & Zhao [30] showed that another method outlined in [6] can have
59: second-order convergence in H γ for u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ+4) with γ ≥ 0. In a more recent arti-
60: cle, Wu & Zhao [31] proposed two embedded low-regularity integrators for the KdV equation,
61: which have first-order convergence inH γ for u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ+1) with γ >1
62: 2 and second-order
63: convergence H γ for u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ+3) with γ ≥ 0, respectively. The minimal regularity re-
64: quirement for the convergence analysis of these unfiltered algorithms for the KdV equation is
65: u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ) for γ >3/2. This condition naturally arises in the energy type of stability
66: analysis.
67: The convergence of a fully discrete finite difference method was proved in [4] for u ∈
68: C([0, T]; H γ) with γ ≥ 3/4 under the CFL condition ∆ t ≤ ∆x3, where ∆ t and ∆ x denote
69: the stepsize and mesh size in the temporal and spatial discretizations, respectively. The CFL
70: condition in a finite difference method plays a similar role as the filters in a spectral method,
71: i.e., to improve the stability of the method under low-regularity conditions. In the case of
72: γ = 3/4, the method is proved convergent with order 1 /42. Since the convergence analysis
73: relies on the smoothing effect on R, the proof cannot be extended to the torus T.
74: Similarly, the development of low-regularity integrators for the NLS equations can be found
75: in [13, 14, 23, 29]. The minimal regularity requirement for the convergence analysis of the
76: unfiltered algorithms for the NLS equation is u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ) for γ > d/2, where d is the
77: dimension of space. This condition also arises in the energy stability analysis, which require
78: using the Kato–Ponce inequality ∥f g∥H γ ≲ ∥f ∥H γ ∥g∥H γ with γ >d

306: The rest of this article is organized as follows. Some basic notations and preliminary results
307: are presented in Section 2. Several new tools for the construction and analysis of low-regularity
308: integrators are presented in Section 3, including a logarithmically growing trilinear estimate
309: on L2, the averaging approximation of exponential functions with imaginary powers, and new
310: trilinear estimates associated to the KdV operator. The construction of the low-regularity
311: integrator is presented in Section 4, and the reduction of the proposed numerical scheme to a
312: continuously formulated perturbed KdV equation is presented in Section 5. The consistency
313: estimates for the local and global errors are presented in Sections 6 and 7, respectively. The
314: stability estimates using low- and high-frequency decompositions are presented in Section 8.
315: The error estimates (i.e., proof of Theorem 1.1), which combine the consistency and stability
316: estimates, are presented in Section 9. Numerical experiments and conclusions are presented
317: in Sections 10 and 11, respectively.

5888: 11. Conclusions and extended studies
5889: We have presented several new tools for the construction and analysis of low-regularity
5890: integrators for the KdV equations, including the averaging approximation technique for ex-
5891: ponential functions with imaginary powers (Lemma 3.2), the new estimates for the symbol
5892: ϕ = k3 − k3
5893: 1 − k3
5894: 2 − k3
5895: 3 (Lemma 3.3), and new trilinear estimates associated to the KdV op-
5896: erator (Proposition 3.4). These new techniques have played essential roles in analyzing the
5897: local error, global remainder, and the stability estimates. We have also introduced a new
5898: technique, which reformulates the numerical scheme into a perturbed integral formulation of
5899: the continuous KdV equation globally posed on the time interval [0 , T], instead of locally
5900: posed on [tn, tn+1], for analyzing the stability of numerical approximations to solutions below
5901: H 1. By combining the several new techniques, we have constructed a new time discretiza-
5902: tion which is convergent with order γ in L2 (up to a logarithmic factor) under the regularity
5903: condition u ∈ C([0, T]; H γ), with γ ∈ (0, 1] possibly approaching zero.
5904: This paper focuses on the development of low-regularity integrators that could improve
5905: the convergence rates of time discretization without the necessity of using filters. Typically,
5906: filters necessitates a stepsize that correlates with the degrees of freedom in space discretization,
5907: similar to a CFL condition. Our approach increases the flexibility in choosing the degrees of
5908: freedom for space discretization, which enables the design of a fully discrete numerical scheme
5909: that operates independently of any CFL condition. We believe that rigorous analysis of the
5910: full discretization, when coupled with the Fourier spectral method in space, can be conducted
5911: within the theoretical framework proposed in this paper, which provides a foundation for such
5912: future research.
5913: The algorithm constructed in this paper improves the error from O(τ γ/3) to O(τ γ ln(1/τ )),
5914: with a logarithmic factor ln(1 /τ ) arising from technical estimates detailed within our paper.
5915: The optimality of the logarithmic factor ln(1 /τ ) is uncertain since the numerical tests cannot
5916: reveal the logarithmic influence on convergence rates. Typically, if the theoretical error is
5917: expressed as O(τ γ−ϵ) for any ϵ in the range (0 , γ), numerical tests would generally reflect a
5918: convergence order of γ. Hence, further study is required to determine if the logarithmic term
5919: can be refined in future analyses.
5920: The methodologies and theoretical framework introduced in this article can be extended
5921: to develop low-regularity integrators for a variety of nonlinear dispersive equations. These in-
5922: clude the modified KdV equation, the generalized KdV equation, and the nonlinear Schr¨ odinger
5923: (NLS) equation. For instance, consider the NLS equation given by
5924: i∂tu + ∂xxu = |u|2u (11.1)
5925: 
5926: 48
5927: This equation can be decomposed into low- and high-frequency components as follows:
5928: (
5929: i∂tu≤N = ∂xxu≤N + λ|u≤N |2u≤N + N1(u≤N , u>N ),
5930: i∂tu>N = ∂xxu>N + 4πλM0u>N + N2(u≤N , u>N ), (11.2)
5931: where u≤N = Π≤N u and u>N = Π>N u. The remainder terms Nj(u≤N , u>N ) for j = 1, 2 can
5932: be addressed by adopting the trilinear estimate strategies developed in Section 3.3 (refer to
5933: the definition of T (v1, v2, v3) and subsequent discussions). Furthermore, the low-frequency
5934: component can be approximated using the averaging approximation techniques described in
5935: this paper. Thus, we can design a low-regularity integrator for the NLS equation that sep-
5936: arately computes the high- and low-frequency parts of the solution, as elaborated in [28].
5937: Employing the framework proposed in Section 5, the numerical scheme can be reduced to
5938: a perturbed integral formulation of the continuous NLS equation. This adaptation enables
5939: the proof of convergence rates using the Strichartz estimates for the continuous NLS equa-
5940: tion, leading to a low-regularity integrator whose L2-norm error is O(τ
5941: 4γ

5943: C([0, T]; H γ). For small values of γ, this convergence rate surpasses those of pre-existing
5944: algorithms; see [28] for more details.

5946: posed framework and techniques, for nonlinear dispersive equations in both one- and higher-
5947: dimensional spaces, will be studied in our future work.

    Title:On the regularization mechanism for the periodic Korteweg-de Vries equation

    Authors:Anatoli V. Babin, Alexei A. Ilyin, Edriss S. Titi
            View a PDF of the paper titled On the regularization mechanism for the periodic Korteweg-de Vries equation, by Anatoli V. Babin and 1 other authors

    View PDF
    HTML (experimental)



    
            Abstract:In this paper we develop and use successive averaging methods for explaining the regularization mechanism in the the periodic Korteweg--de Vries (KdV) equation in the homogeneous Sobolev spaces $\dot{H}^s$, for $s\ge0$. Specifically, we prove the global existence, uniqueness, and Lipschitz continuous dependence on the initial data of the solutions of the periodic KdV. For the case where the initial data is in $L_2$ we also show the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these solutions with respect to the initial data as maps from $\dot{H}^s$ to $\dot{H}^s$, for $s\in(-1,0]$.

                    Abstract
This article is concerned with the construction and analysis of new time discretizations for the KdV equation on a torus for low-regularity solutions below \(H^1\). New harmonic analysis tools, including averaging approximations to the exponential phase functions and trilinear estimates of the KdV operator, are established for the construction and analysis of time discretizations with higher convergence orders under low-regularity conditions. In addition, new perturbation techniques are introduced to establish stability estimates of time discretizations under low-regularity conditions without using filters when the energy techniques fail. The proposed method is proved to be convergent with order \(\gamma \) (up to a logarithmic factor) in \(L^2\) under the regularity condition \(u\in C([0,T];H^\gamma )\) for \(\gamma \in (0,1]\).

For tau>0, t_n=n*tau and k!=0, hat(R2_(n,tau)(f1,f2,f3))(k)= -tau/(18*i*k) sum_(a+b+c=k,a+b!=0) exp(-i*t_n*Phi)*eta_tau(alpha,beta)*hat f1(a)*hat f2(b)*hat f3(c), with p=a+b, alpha=3*a*b*p, beta=3*k*c*p, Phi=alpha+beta=k^3-a^3-b^3-c^3. Output at k=0 is zero. Initially this formula is on Fourier polynomials; bounded extension is proved below. Terms with a zero input frequency vanish since one phase is zero.
B_t(f,g)=S_(-t) partial_x[(S_t f)(S_t g)].
J_t(f,g)=S_(-t) P[(S_t Dinv f)(S_t Dinv g)].
For I=[a,b] with 0<=a<=b, Cint_I(f,g,h)=integral_I S_(-t) P{P[(S_t f(t))(S_t g(t))]*(S_t Dinv h(t))}dt; time-independent inputs are read as constant paths.
p_star=23/14. For an interval I of length at most one, ||f||_X(I)=||f||_(L^infty(I;L2))+||partial_t f||_(L^infty(I;H^(-p_star))).

binders.type: time path with the displayed norms finite

record.definition: For 0<gamma<=1, a_gamma=1/2-gamma if gamma<1/2; a_gamma=1/8 if gamma=1/2; and a_gamma=0 if gamma>1/2.

For tau>0, nonnegative integer n, t_n=n*tau and t in [t_n,t_n+tau], Stage_(n,tau)(t;f)= (1/2) integral_(t_n)^t B_s(f,f)ds, initially for a time-independent smooth mean-zero f; the endpoint normal form below gives its L2 extension.

For smooth mean-zero step data f at t_n=n*tau, write F_n(t)=Stage_(n,tau)(t;f), z_n=f+F_n, C_n(t)=integral_(t_n)^t B_s(f,F_n(s))ds, Q_n(t)=(1/2)integral_(t_n)^t B_s(F_n(s),F_n(s))ds, W_n=Q_n(t_n+tau)+R2_(n,tau)(f,f,f), V_n(t)=f+F_n(t)+C_n(t)+Q_n(t)-(t-t_n)*W_n/tau, Y_n=V_n-z_n, rho_n(t)=-integral_(t_n)^t B_s(Y_n,z_n)ds-(1/2)integral_(t_n)^t B_s(Y_n,Y_n)ds-(t-t_n)*W_n/tau. For f=S_(-t_n)u^n, concatenate V_n as V and the increments rho_n as Rres, with Rres(0)=0. Continuity of V at grid points is a proved property, not an assumption.
